final_candidates.decision_summary: R157Q is a well-established severe loss-of-function mutation in human MTHFR that abolishes catalytic activity while preserving protein fold integrity.
D188 acts as a critical catalytic active-site residue; substitution with alanine directly eliminates enzymatic turnover.
Alanine substitution at R157 strips the essential positive charge and hydrogen bonding required for substrate/cofactor binding, abolishing activity.

stop_reason.detail: High-confidence active site loss-of-function candidates identified and prioritized; additional self-iteration is not required.

history.rationale: D188 serves as the primary catalytic acid/base in the MTHFR active site. Mutation to alanine removes the essential carboxylate required for proton transfer, abolishing catalytic activity while maintaining structural stability.
D188 is a critical catalytic acid/base residue in the active site TIM barrel; alanine substitution directly abolishes enzymatic activity.

Arg157 is an essential residue in the catalytic pocket that coordinates the cofactor and substrate. Substitution with glutamine is a clinically validated severe loss-of-function mutation causing near-complete loss of enzymatic activity.

R157Q is a well-characterized severe clinical loss-of-function mutation in human MTHFR that drastically impairs catalysis while preserving folding. It merits the top ranking for reliably abolishing activity.

Arg157 forms critical electrostatic contacts with the cofactor/substrate in the active site. Alanine substitution disrupts these required interactions, eliminating catalytic function without disrupting the overall fold.
Alanine scanning at Arg157 eliminates the key electrostatic contacts required for cofactor/substrate binding, completely crippling catalytic turnover.
Tyr189 provides essential aromatic stacking for substrate orientation in the catalytic pocket. Alanine substitution eliminates this interaction, abolishing substrate binding and enzymatic turnover.
Y189 participates directly in active site aromatic stacking and transition state stabilization. Alanine mutation disrupts the catalytic pocket.
Asp191 is an active-site carboxylate coordinating the catalytic hydrogen-bonding network. Mutating it to alanine disrupts active site organization and abolishes catalytic efficiency.
D191 contributes to the active site electrostatic network; mutation significantly reduces MTHFR activity.

His263 is a conserved catalytic cleft histidine involved in the active site proton-relay and transition-state stabilization. Mutation to alanine severely impairs hydride transfer and eliminates activity.
H263 coordinates active site cofactor interactions; substitution compromises catalytic efficiency.
Trp95 lines the active-site cavity and is critical for defining the substrate-binding pocket geometry. Trp-to-Ala substitution compromises cofactor/substrate positioning, leading to loss of function.
W95 forms part of the conserved folate-binding cleft, and mutation severely disrupts folate affinity.

Asp159 is part of the conserved active-site loop directly adjacent to Arg158/Arg157. Alanine substitution disrupts the local loop conformation and active-site architecture, severely impairing function.
D159 is involved in binding domain loop stability, where mutation lowers enzymatic performance.
